g.text: The modelling decision and the concurrency mechanism are the same decision
Inventory is a COUNTER rather than a set of room states - which is exactly what makes a single atomic UPDATE sufficient.
used at CHECK-IN and by housekeeping -
NOT involved in booking at all
the backstop that no code path can bypass
THE CENTRAL TABLE one row per (hotel, room type, date)
end_date is EXCLUSIVE: 2026-06-01 to 2026-06-04 is THREE nights, and the guest
checks out on the 4th. Not pedantry - it removes a class of off-by-one bug.
Half-open intervals make the predicate date >= start AND date < end with no -1
anywhere, make the night count a plain subtraction, and make two consecutive stays
NOT overlap when one's end equals the other's start. An inclusive end_date needs
date <= end - 1 in every query, and somebody eventually forgets the -1 and
reserves a room for the checkout night.
The obvious model, and why it is wrong for this product
CREATE TABLE room_night (hotel_id, room_id, date, reservation_id NULL, ...);
Guests book a room TYPE, and the front desk assigns a specific room at check-in - so which physical room is involved is
unknown at booking time and irrelevant until arrival. Modelling per-room would force the booking transaction to PICK a room:
a scan plus a decision, with two concurrent bookings contending over arbitrary specific rows. Worse, assigning room 412 at
booking time removes the front desk's flexibility to reshuffle for maintenance, adjacency requests or an early checkout.
Modelling it as a counter makes the booking a single arithmetic update - and that is precisely what makes the atomic
conditional UPDATE available as the concurrency mechanism. THE DATA MODEL CHOICE IS WHAT UNLOCKED THE SIMPLEST CORRECT
CONCURRENCY CONTROL. The room table still exists, because check-in and housekeeping need it; it just isn't involved in
PRIMARY KEY (hotel_id, room_type_id, date) - and the order is load-bearing
WHERE hotel_id = 245 AND room_type_id = 1001 AND date >= '2026-06-01' AND date < '2026-06-04'
date LAST -> one B-tree descent plus a short sequential scan
All of one room type's dates are physically contiguous, so a stay of any
length is one descent and a short scan - true for BOTH the availability
read and the booking UPDATE, which is why the booking transaction is
short enough to make locking a non-issue. The range scan also gives lock
date FIRST -> 14 separate index probes for a 14-night stay
Reverse the order and one room type's nights scatter across the index by
date - so the UPDATE locks 14 rows in unpredictable physical locations,
which is exactly the deadlock exposure that pessimistic locking warns
about. The same key order that makes the read fast is the one that makes
Two decisions that look like ordinary normalization and are not
rates live in their own table, keyed by date
Prices change daily, so rate cannot be a column on room_type - that would store one price for all time. But it is also a
SEPARATE TABLE FROM INVENTORY rather than another column on the inventory row, for an ownership reason as much as a technical
one: rates are set by revenue management on their own cadence and tooling, while inventory is mutated by the booking path
thousands of times more often. Putting the rate on the inventory row would mean every price change writes to THE ROW THAT
BOOKINGS CONTEND ON - adding write contention to the hottest row in the system, for data the booking transaction only reads.
rate_minor is an integer of minor units: a total assembled from 14 nightly rates would accumulate float representation error
into a figure somebody gets charged.
expires_at exists to drive the sweeper
Set when a reservation is created as pending, cleared on confirmation. The mechanism matters: PENDING RESERVATIONS HOLD
INVENTORY. A checkout abandoned at the payment step has already incremented total_reserved, so without a sweeper that
inventory is held forever, and the failure mode is availability slowly leaking away - a hotel that looks full and isn't, with
nothing in the logs to explain it. So the alert is not on the sweeper's completion; it is on INVENTORY CURRENTLY HELD BY
PENDING ROWS. That is the number that says whether the mechanism is working.
Indexes - and one partial index worth the detail
PRIMARY KEY (hotel_id, room_type_id, date) on room_type_inventory the availability range scan AND the booking UPDATE, both
as one descent plus a short scan. The most important index
PRIMARY KEY (reservation_id) on reservation lookup by id - and the uniqueness that IS idempotency
INDEX (guest_id, created_at DESC) on reservation 'my bookings, newest first'. DESC means no sort.
INDEX (hotel_id, start_date) on reservation the front desk's arrivals list, and check-in assignment
INDEX (status, expires_at) WHERE status = 'pending' THE SWEEPER'S SCAN, and partial on purpose: the
overwhelming majority of rows are terminal and are not
indexed at all. A full index would grow with total booking
volume to serve a query that only ever wants the handful
PRIMARY KEY (hotel_id, room_type_id, date) on room_type_rate co-ordered with inventory, so a stay's rates are also one
spatial index on (latitude, longitude) on hotel search by location - a single-column index on lat OR lng
Deliberately absent: nothing on total_reserved or total_inventory - they are read as part of the row, never searched by.
Nothing on reservation.status alone (cardinality 4, so the planner would ignore it). And no index on room.room_type_id,
because room assignment is per-hotel and a hotel has tens of rooms, not millions.
The same data has different consistency requirements depending on whether it is DISPLAYED or DECIDED ON
room_type_inventory, the write STRONG, serializable in effect where double-booking is prevented: the atomic conditional
UPDATE plus the CHECK backstop. Non-negotiable.
room_type_inventory, the read EVENTUAL, from a replica availability SHOWN to a browsing user may be stale, because
the authoritative check happens again in the transaction
reservation STRONG, read-your-writes a guest who just booked must see it - and a stale read on
reservation_id would defeat idempotency, creating a second
status transitions STRONG a lost pending -> confirmed leaves a PAID reservation
unconfirmed while the sweeper releases its inventory
hotel / room_type / room EVENTUAL, long TTL near-static; a description a few minutes stale is invisible.
The highest-volume read path, and it caches almost perfectly.
room_type_rate STRONG at booking, eventual for display a price shown while browsing may be stale; the
price CHARGED must be the one read inside the transaction,
or you charge a rate the user never saw
the inventory cache (at scale) EVENTUAL, CDC-fed the database remains the authority, so staleness can only
cause a misleading display, never an oversell
Availability, rates and inventory each appear TWICE in that list with different models. Getting that distinction right is what
lets a system with a hard correctness requirement still serve 1,000x more reads than writes from replicas and caches.
If it had to scale: shard on hotel_id - an unusually clean story, and a property of the DOMAIN
Every query filters on hotel_id, so the shard is computable from the
request: single-shard reads and writes, always. And critically, NO
TRANSACTION EVER SPANS TWO HOTELS - a booking touches exactly one
hotel's inventory - so there are no distributed transactions at all.
The cost: a query spanning many hotels (a city search results page)
becomes a scatter-gather. Acceptable, because hotel SEARCH is served by
a separate search index, not by scanning the inventory table.
all bookings for peak season concentrate on one shard, and the
current date's shard takes every check-in query. A hotspot on both axes.
distributes reservations perfectly and SCATTERS ONE HOTEL'S INVENTORY
across every shard, so the booking transaction becomes distributed. Fatal.
wildly skewed, and it makes hotel counts per shard depend on tourism
And the inventory cache, if added, is DISPLAY-ONLY: key {hotel_id}_{room_type_id}_{date} -> available_count, fed by CDC from
the replication log. A stale cache can make a user see '1 room left' and then receive a 409 - mildly annoying, and IDENTICAL
to what already happens when somebody hesitates while browsing and somebody else books first. It cannot cause an oversell,
because the atomic UPDATE and the CHECK constraint are still the gate. That is why cache/database inconsistency is tolerable
here when it would be unacceptable in the digital wallet: THE CACHE NEVER PARTICIPATES IN THE DECISION.
